rows.heading: Extend the properties of exponents to rational exponents.
rows.statement: Explain how the definition of the meaning of rational exponents follows from extending the properties of integer exponents to those values, allowing for a notation for radicals in terms of rational exponents. For example, we define 5^(1/3) to be the cube root of 5 because we want (5^(1/3))^3 = 5^((1/3)3) to hold, so (5^(1/3))^3 must equal 5.

rows.heading: Extend the properties of exponents to rational exponents.
rows.statement: Rewrite expressions involving radicals and rational exponents using the properties of exponents.

rows.heading: Use properties of rational and irrational numbers.
rows.statement: Explain why the sum or product of two rational numbers is rational; that the sum of a rational number and an irrational number is irrational; and that the product of a nonzero rational number and an irrational number is irrational.

rows.heading: Reason quantitatively and use units to solve problems.
rows.statement: Use units as a way to understand problems and to guide the solution of multi-step problems; choose and interpret units consistently in formulas; choose and interpret the scale and the origin in graphs and data displays.

rows.heading: Reason quantitatively and use units to solve problems.
rows.statement: Define appropriate quantities for the purpose of descriptive modeling.

rows.heading: Reason quantitatively and use units to solve problems.
rows.statement: Choose a level of accuracy appropriate to limitations on measurement when reporting quantities.

rows.heading: Perform arithmetic operations with complex numbers.
rows.statement: Know there is a complex number i such that i^2 = -1, and every complex number has the form a + bi with a and b real.

rows.heading: Perform arithmetic operations with complex numbers.
rows.statement: Use the relation i^2 = -1 and the commutative, associative, and distributive properties to add, subtract, and multiply complex numbers.

rows.heading: Perform arithmetic operations with complex numbers.
rows.statement: (+) Find the conjugate of a complex number; use conjugates to find moduli and quotients of complex numbers.

rows.heading: Represent complex numbers and their operations on the complex plane.
rows.statement: (+) Represent complex numbers on the complex plane in rectangular and polar form (including real and imaginary numbers), and explain why the rectangular and polar forms of a given complex number represent the same number.

rows.heading: Represent complex numbers and their operations on the complex plane.
rows.statement: (+) Represent addition, subtraction, multiplication, and conjugation of complex numbers geometrically on the complex plane; use properties of this representation for computation. For example, (-1 + √3 i)^3 = 8 because (-1 + √3 i) has modulus 2 and argument 120°.

rows.heading: Represent complex numbers and their operations on the complex plane.
rows.statement: (+) Calculate the distance between numbers in the complex plane as the modulus of the difference, and the midpoint of a segment as the average of the numbers at its endpoints.

rows.heading: Use complex numbers in polynomial identities and equations.
rows.statement: Solve quadratic equations with real coefficients that have complex solutions.

rows.heading: Use complex numbers in polynomial identities and equations.
rows.statement: (+) Extend polynomial identities to the complex numbers. For example, rewrite x^2 + 4 as (x + 2i)(x - 2i).

rows.heading: Use complex numbers in polynomial identities and equations.
rows.statement: (+) Know the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra; show that it is true for quadratic polynomials.

rows.heading: Represent and model with vector quantities.
rows.statement: (+) Recognize vector quantities as having both magnitude and direction. Represent vector quantities by directed line segments, and use appropriate symbols for vectors and their magnitudes (e.g., v, |v|, ||v||, v).

rows.heading: Represent and model with vector quantities.
rows.statement: (+) Find the components of a vector by subtracting the coordinates of an initial point from the coordinates of a terminal point.

rows.heading: Represent and model with vector quantities.
rows.statement: (+) Solve problems involving velocity and other quantities that can be represented by vectors.

rows.heading: Perform operations on vectors.
rows.statement: (+) Add and subtract vectors.

rows.heading: Perform operations on vectors.
rows.statement: Add vectors end-to-end, component-wise, and by the parallelogram rule. Understand that the magnitude of a sum of two vectors is typically not the sum of the magnitudes.

rows.heading: Perform operations on vectors.
rows.statement: Given two vectors in magnitude and direction form, determine the magnitude and direction of their sum.

rows.heading: Perform operations on vectors.
rows.statement: Understand vector subtraction v - w as v + (-w), where -w is the additive inverse of w, with the same magnitude as w and pointing in the opposite direction. Represent vector subtraction graphically by connecting the tips in the appropriate order, and perform vector subtraction component-wise.

rows.heading: Perform operations on vectors.
rows.statement: (+) Multiply a vector by a scalar.

rows.heading: Perform operations on vectors.
rows.statement: Represent scalar multiplication graphically by scaling vectors and possibly reversing their direction; perform scalar multiplication component-wise, e.g., as c(v_x, v_y) = (cv_x, cv_y).

rows.heading: Perform operations on vectors.
rows.statement: Compute the magnitude of a scalar multiple cv using ||cv|| = |c|v. Compute the direction of cv knowing that when |c|v ≠ 0, the direction of cv is either along v (for c > 0) or against v (for c < 0).

rows.heading: Perform operations on matrices and use matrices in applications.
rows.statement: (+) Use matrices to represent and manipulate data, e.g., to represent payoffs or incidence relationships in a network.

rows.heading: Perform operations on matrices and use matrices in applications.
rows.statement: (+) Multiply matrices by scalars to produce new matrices, e.g., as when all of the payoffs in a game are doubled.

rows.heading: Perform operations on matrices and use matrices in applications.
rows.statement: (+) Add, subtract, and multiply matrices of appropriate dimensions.

rows.heading: Perform operations on matrices and use matrices in applications.
rows.statement: (+) Understand that, unlike multiplication of numbers, matrix multiplication for square matrices is not a commutative operation, but still satisfies the associative and distributive properties.

rows.heading: Perform operations on matrices and use matrices in applications.
rows.statement: (+) Understand that the zero and identity matrices play a role in matrix addition and multiplication similar to the role of 0 and 1 in the real numbers. The determinant of a square matrix is nonzero if and only if the matrix has a multiplicative inverse.

rows.heading: Perform operations on matrices and use matrices in applications.
rows.statement: (+) Multiply a vector (regarded as a matrix with one column) by a matrix of suitable dimensions to produce another vector. Work with matrices as transformations of vectors.

rows.heading: Perform operations on matrices and use matrices in applications.
Interpret the structure of expressions.
rows.statement: Interpret expressions that represent a quantity in terms of its context.

rows.heading: Interpret the structure of expressions.
rows.statement: Interpret parts of an expression, such as terms, factors, and coefficients.

rows.heading: Interpret the structure of expressions.
rows.statement: Interpret complicated expressions by viewing one or more of their parts as a single entity. For example, interpret P(1+r)^n as the product of P and a factor not depending on P.

rows.heading: Interpret the structure of expressions.
rows.statement: Use the structure of an expression to identify ways to rewrite it. For example, see x^4 - y^4 as (x^2)^2 - (y^2)^2, thus recognizing it as a difference of squares that can be factored as (x^2 - y^2)(x^2 + y^2).

rows.heading: Write expressions in equivalent forms to solve problems.
rows.statement: Choose and produce an equivalent form of an expression to reveal and explain properties of the quantity represented by the expression.

rows.heading: Write expressions in equivalent forms to solve problems.
rows.statement: Factor a quadratic expression to reveal the zeros of the function it defines.

rows.heading: Write expressions in equivalent forms to solve problems.
rows.statement: Complete the square in a quadratic expression to reveal the maximum or minimum value of the function it defines.

rows.heading: Write expressions in equivalent forms to solve problems.
rows.statement: Use the properties of exponents to transform expressions for exponential functions. For example the expression 1.15^t can be rewritten as (1.15^(1/12))^12t ≈ 1.012^12t to reveal the approximate equivalent monthly interest rate if the annual rate is 15%.

rows.heading: Write expressions in equivalent forms to solve problems.
rows.statement: Derive the formula for the sum of a finite geometric series (when the common ratio is not 1), and use the formula to solve problems. For example, calculate mortgage payments.

rows.heading: Perform arithmetic operations on polynomials.
rows.statement: Understand that polynomials form a system analogous to the integers, namely, they are closed under the operations of addition, subtraction, and multiplication; add, subtract, and multiply polynomials.

rows.heading: Understand the relationship between zeros and factors of polynomials.
rows.statement: Know and apply the Remainder Theorem: For a polynomial p(x) and a number a, the remainder on division by x - a is p(a), so p(a) = 0 if and only if (x - a) is a factor of p(x).

rows.heading: Understand the relationship between zeros and factors of polynomials.
rows.statement: Identify zeros of polynomials when suitable factorizations are available, and use the zeros to construct a rough graph of the function defined by the polynomial.

rows.heading: Use polynomial identities to solve problems.
rows.statement: Prove polynomial identities and use them to describe numerical relationships. For example, the polynomial identity (x^2 + y^2)^2 = (x^2 - y^2)^2 + (2xy)^2 can be used to generate Pythagorean triples.

rows.heading: Use polynomial identities to solve problems.
rows.statement: (+) Know and apply the Binomial Theorem for the expansion of (x + y)^n in powers of x and y for a positive integer n, where x and y are any numbers, with coefficients determined for example by Pascal's Triangle.

rows.heading: Rewrite rational expressions.
rows.statement: Rewrite simple rational expressions in different forms; write a(x)/b(x) in the form q(x) + r(x)/b(x), where a(x), b(x), q(x), and r(x) are polynomials with the degree of r(x) less than the degree of b(x), using inspection, long division, or, for the more complicated examples, a computer algebra system.

rows.heading: Rewrite rational expressions.
rows.statement: (+) Understand that rational expressions form a system analogous to the rational numbers, closed under addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division by a nonzero rational expression; add, subtract, multiply, and divide rational expressions.

rows.heading: Create equations that describe numbers or relationships.
rows.statement: Create equations and inequalities in one variable and use them to solve problems. Include equations arising from linear and quadratic functions, and simple rational and exponential functions.

rows.heading: Create equations that describe numbers or relationships.
rows.statement: Create equations in two or more variables to represent relationships between quantities; graph equations on coordinate axes with labels and scales.

rows.heading: Create equations that describe numbers or relationships.
rows.statement: Represent constraints by equations or inequalities, and by systems of equations and/or inequalities, and interpret solutions as viable or nonviable options in a modeling context. For example, represent inequalities describing nutritional and cost constraints on combinations of different foods.

rows.heading: Create equations that describe numbers or relationships.
rows.statement: Rearrange formulas to highlight a quantity of interest, using the same reasoning as in solving equations. For example, rearrange Ohm's law V = IR to highlight resistance R.

rows.heading: Understand solving equations as a process of reasoning and explain the reasoning.
rows.statement: Explain each step in solving a simple equation as following from the equality of numbers asserted at the previous step, starting from the assumption that the original equation has a solution. Construct a viable argument to justify a solution method.

rows.heading: Understand solving equations as a process of reasoning and explain the reasoning.
rows.statement: Solve simple rational and radical equations in one variable, and give examples showing how extraneous solutions may arise.

rows.heading: Solve equations and inequalities in one variable.
rows.statement: Solve linear equations and inequalities in one variable, including equations with coefficients represented by letters.

rows.heading: Solve equations and inequalities in one variable.
rows.statement: Solve quadratic equations in one variable.

rows.heading: Solve equations and inequalities in one variable.
rows.statement: Use the method of completing the square to transform any quadratic equation in x into an equation of the form (x - p)^2 = q that has the same solutions. Derive the quadratic formula from this form.

rows.heading: Solve equations and inequalities in one variable.
Solve systems of equations.
rows.statement: Prove that, given a system of two equations in two variables, replacing one equation by the sum of that equation and a multiple of the other produces a system with the same solutions.

rows.heading: Solve systems of equations.
rows.statement: Solve systems of linear equations exactly and approximately (e.g., with graphs), focusing on pairs of linear equations in two variables.

rows.heading: Solve systems of equations.
rows.statement: Solve a simple system consisting of a linear equation and a quadratic equation in two variables algebraically and graphically. For example, find the points of intersection between the line y = -3x and the circle x^2 + y^2 = 3.

rows.heading: Solve systems of equations.
rows.statement: (+) Represent a system of linear equations as a single matrix equation in a vector variable.

rows.heading: Solve systems of equations.
rows.statement: (+) Find the inverse of a matrix if it exists and use it to solve systems of linear equations (using technology for matrices of dimension 3 × 3 or greater).

rows.heading: Represent and solve equations and inequalities graphically.
rows.statement: Understand that the graph of an equation in two variables is the set of all its solutions plotted in the coordinate plane, often forming a curve (which could be a line).

rows.heading: Represent and solve equations and inequalities graphically.
rows.statement: Explain why the x-coordinates of the points where the graphs of the equations y = f(x) and y = g(x) intersect are the solutions of the equation f(x) = g(x); find the solutions approximately, e.g., using technology to graph the functions, make tables of values, or find successive approximations. Include cases where f(x) and/or g(x) are linear, polynomial, rational, absolute value, exponential, and logarithmic functions.

rows.heading: Represent and solve equations and inequalities graphically.
rows.statement: Graph the solutions to a linear inequality in two variables as a half-plane (excluding the boundary in the case of a strict inequality), and graph the solution set to a system of linear inequalities in two variables as the intersection of the corresponding half-planes.

rows.heading: Understand the concept of a function and use function notation.
rows.statement: Understand that a function from one set (called the domain) to another set (called the range) assigns to each element of the domain exactly one element of the range. If f is a function and x is an element of its domain, then f(x) denotes the output of f corresponding to the input x. The graph of f is the graph of the equation y = f(x).

rows.heading: Understand the concept of a function and use function notation.
rows.statement: Use function notation, evaluate functions for inputs in their domains, and interpret statements that use function notation in terms of a context.

rows.heading: Understand the concept of a function and use function notation.
rows.statement: Recognize that sequences are functions, sometimes defined recursively, whose domain is a subset of the integers. For example, the Fibonacci sequence is defined recursively by f(0) = f(1) = 1, f(n+1) = f(n) + f(n-1) for n ≥ 1.

rows.heading: Interpret functions that arise in applications in terms of the context.
rows.statement: For a function that models a relationship between two quantities, interpret key features of graphs and tables in terms of the quantities, and sketch graphs showing key features given a verbal description of the relationship. Key features include: intercepts; intervals where the function is increasing, decreasing, positive, or negative; relative maximums and minimums; symmetries; end behavior; and periodicity.

rows.heading: Interpret functions that arise in applications in terms of the context.
rows.statement: Relate the domain of a function to its graph and, where applicable, to the quantitative relationship it describes. For example, if the function h(n) gives the number of person-hours it takes to assemble n engines in a factory, then the positive integers would be an appropriate domain for the function.

rows.heading: Interpret functions that arise in applications in terms of the context.
rows.statement: Calculate and interpret the average rate of change of a function (presented symbolically or as a table) over a specified interval. Estimate the rate of change from a graph.

rows.heading: Analyze functions using different representations.
rows.statement: Graph functions expressed symbolically and show key features of the graph, by hand in simple cases and using technology for more complicated cases.

rows.heading: Analyze functions using different representations.
rows.statement: Graph linear and quadratic functions and show intercepts, maxima, and minima.

rows.heading: Analyze functions using different representations.
rows.statement: Graph square root, cube root, and piecewise-defined functions, including step functions and absolute value functions.

rows.heading: Analyze functions using different representations.
rows.statement: Graph polynomial functions, identifying zeros when suitable factorizations are available, and showing end behavior.

rows.heading: Analyze functions using different representations.
rows.statement: (+) Graph rational functions, identifying zeros and asymptotes when suitable factorizations are available, and showing end behavior.

rows.heading: Analyze functions using different representations.
rows.statement: Graph exponential and logarithmic functions, showing intercepts and end behavior, and trigonometric functions, showing period, midline, and amplitude.

rows.heading: Analyze functions using different representations.
rows.statement: Write a function defined by an expression in different but equivalent forms to reveal and explain different properties of the function.

rows.heading: Analyze functions using different representations.
rows.statement: Use the process of factoring and completing the square in a quadratic function to show zeros, extreme values, and symmetry of the graph, and interpret these in terms of a context.

rows.heading: Analyze functions using different representations.
rows.statement: Use the properties of exponents to interpret expressions for exponential functions. For example, identify percent rate of change in functions such as y = (1.02)ᵗ, y = (0.97)ᵗ, y = (1.01)12ᵗ, y = (1.2)ᵗ/10, and classify them as representing exponential growth or decay.

rows.heading: Analyze functions using different representations.
rows.statement: Compare properties of two functions each represented in a different way (algebraically, graphically, numerically in tables, or by verbal descriptions). For example, given a graph of one quadratic function and an algebraic expression for another, say which has the larger maximum.

rows.heading: Build a function that models a relationship between two quantities.
rows.statement: Write a function that describes a relationship between two quantities.

rows.heading: Build a function that models a relationship between two quantities.
rows.statement: Determine an explicit expression, a recursive process, or steps for calculation from a context.

rows.heading: Build a function that models a relationship between two quantities.
rows.statement: Combine standard function types using arithmetic operations. For example, build a function that models the temperature of a cooling body by adding a constant function to a decaying exponential, and relate these functions to the model.

rows.heading: Build a function that models a relationship between two quantities.
rows.statement: (+) Compose functions. For example, if T(y) is the temperature in the atmosphere as a function of height, and h(t) is the height of a weather balloon as a function of time, then T(h(t)) is the temperature at the location of the weather balloon as a function of time.

rows.heading: Build a function that models a relationship between two quantities.
rows.statement: Write arithmetic and geometric sequences both recursively and with an explicit formula, use them to model situations, and translate between the two forms.

rows.heading: Build new functions from existing functions.
rows.statement: Identify the effect on the graph of replacing f(x) by f(x) + k, k f(x), f(kx), and f(x + k) for specific values of k (both positive and negative); find the value of k given the graphs. Experiment with cases and illustrate an explanation of the effects on the graph using technology. Include recognizing even and odd functions from their graphs and algebraic expressions for them.

rows.heading: Build new functions from existing functions.
rows.statement: Find inverse functions.

rows.heading: Build new functions from existing functions.
rows.statement: Solve an equation of the form f(x) = c for a simple function f that has an inverse and write an expression for the inverse. For example, f(x) =2 x^3 or f(x) = (x+1)/(x-1) for x ≠ 1.

rows.heading: Build new functions from existing functions.
rows.statement: (+) Verify by composition that one function is the inverse of another.

rows.heading: Build new functions from existing functions.
rows.statement: (+) Read values of an inverse function from a graph or a table, given that the function has an inverse.

rows.heading: Build new functions from existing functions.
rows.statement: (+) Produce an invertible function from a non-invertible function by restricting the domain.

rows.heading: Build new functions from existing functions.
rows.statement: (+) Understand the inverse relationship between exponents and logarithms and use this relationship to solve problems involving logarithms and exponents.

rows.heading: Construct and compare linear, quadratic, and exponential models and solve problems.
rows.statement: Distinguish between situations that can be modeled with linear functions and with exponential functions.

rows.heading: Construct and compare linear, quadratic, and exponential models and solve problems.
rows.statement: Prove that linear functions grow by equal differences over equal intervals, and that exponential functions grow by equal factors over equal intervals.

rows.heading: Construct and compare linear, quadratic, and exponential models and solve problems.
rows.statement: Recognize situations in which one quantity changes at a constant rate per unit interval relative to another.

rows.heading: Construct and compare linear, quadratic, and exponential models and solve problems.
rows.statement: Recognize situations in which a quantity grows or decays by a constant percent rate per unit interval relative to another.

rows.heading: Construct and compare linear, quadratic, and exponential models and solve problems.
rows.statement: Construct linear and exponential functions, including arithmetic and geometric sequences, given a graph, a description of a relationship, or two input-output pairs (include reading these from a table).

rows.heading: Construct and compare linear, quadratic, and exponential models and solve problems.
rows.statement: Observe using graphs and tables that a quantity increasing exponentially eventually exceeds a quantity increasing linearly, quadratically, or (more generally) as a polynomial function.

rows.heading: Construct and compare linear, quadratic, and exponential models and solve problems.
rows.statement: For exponential models, express as a logarithm the solution to ab^ct = d where a, c, and d are numbers and the base b is 2, 10, or e; evaluate the logarithm using technology.

rows.heading: Interpret expressions for functions in terms of the situation they model.
rows.statement: Interpret the parameters in a linear or exponential function in terms of a context.

rows.heading: Extend the domain of trigonometric functions using the unit circle.
rows.statement: Understand radian measure of an angle as the length of the arc on the unit circle subtended by the angle.

rows.heading: Extend the domain of trigonometric functions using the unit circle.
rows.statement: Explain how the unit circle in the coordinate plane enables the extension of trigonometric functions to all real numbers, interpreted as radian measures of angles traversed counterclockwise around the unit circle.

rows.heading: Extend the domain of trigonometric functions using the unit circle.
Extend the domain of trigonometric functions using the unit circle.
rows.statement: (+) Use the unit circle to explain symmetry (odd and even) and periodicity of trigonometric functions.

rows.heading: Model periodic phenomena with trigonometric functions.
rows.statement: Choose trigonometric functions to model periodic phenomena with specified amplitude, frequency, and midline.

rows.heading: Model periodic phenomena with trigonometric functions.
rows.statement: (+) Understand that restricting a trigonometric function to a domain on which it is always increasing or always decreasing allows its inverse to be constructed.

rows.heading: Model periodic phenomena with trigonometric functions.
rows.statement: (+) Use inverse functions to solve trigonometric equations that arise in modeling contexts; evaluate the solutions using technology, and interpret them in terms of the context.

rows.heading: Prove and apply trigonometric identities.
rows.statement: Prove the Pythagorean identity sin^2(θ) + cos^2(θ) = 1 and use it to find sin(θ), cos(θ), or tan(θ) given sin(θ), cos(θ), or tan(θ) and the quadrant of the angle.

rows.heading: Prove and apply trigonometric identities.
rows.statement: (+) Prove the addition and subtraction formulas for sine, cosine, and tangent and use them to solve problems.

rows.heading: Experiment with transformations in the plane
rows.statement: Know precise definitions of angle, circle, perpendicular line, parallel line, and line segment, based on the undefined notions of point, line, distance along a line, and distance around a circular arc.

rows.heading: Experiment with transformations in the plane
rows.statement: Represent transformations in the plane using, e.g., transparencies and geometry software; describe transformations as functions that take points in the plane as inputs and give other points as outputs. Compare transformations that preserve distance and angle to those that do not (e.g., translation versus horizontal stretch).

rows.heading: Experiment with transformations in the plane
rows.statement: Given a rectangle, parallelogram, trapezoid, or regular polygon, describe the rotations and reflections that carry it onto itself.

rows.heading: Experiment with transformations in the plane
rows.statement: Develop definitions of rotations, reflections, and translations in terms of angles, circles, perpendicular lines, parallel lines, and line segments.

rows.heading: Experiment with transformations in the plane
rows.statement: Given a geometric figure and a rotation, reflection, or translation, draw the transformed figure using, e.g., graph paper, tracing paper, or geometry software. Specify a sequence of transformations that will carry a given figure onto another.

rows.heading: Understand congruence in terms of rigid motions
rows.statement: Use geometric descriptions of rigid motions to transform figures and to predict the effect of a given rigid motion on a given figure; given two figures, use the definition of congruence in terms of rigid motions to decide if they are congruent.

rows.heading: Understand congruence in terms of rigid motions
rows.statement: Use the definition of congruence in terms of rigid motions to show that two triangles are congruent if and only if corresponding pairs of sides and corresponding pairs of angles are congruent.

rows.heading: Understand congruence in terms of rigid motions
rows.statement: Explain how the criteria for triangle congruence (ASA, SAS, and SSS) follow from the definition of congruence in terms of rigid motions.

rows.heading: Prove geometric theorems
rows.statement: Prove theorems about lines and angles. Theorems include: vertical angles are congruent; when a transversal crosses parallel lines, alternate interior angles are congruent and corresponding angles are congruent; points on a perpendicular bisector of a line segment are exactly those equidistant from the segment's endpoints.

rows.heading: Prove geometric theorems
rows.statement: Prove theorems about triangles. Theorems include: measures of interior angles of a triangle sum to 180°; base angles of isosceles triangles are congruent; the segment joining midpoints of two sides of a triangle is parallel to the third side and half the length; the medians of a triangle meet at a point.

rows.heading: Prove geometric theorems
rows.statement: Prove theorems about parallelograms. Theorems include: opposite sides are congruent, opposite angles are congruent, the diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other, and conversely, rectangles are parallelograms with congruent diagonals.

rows.heading: Make geometric constructions
rows.statement: Make formal geometric constructions with a variety of tools and methods (compass and straightedge, string, reflective devices, paper folding, dynamic geometric software, etc.). Copying a segment; copying an angle; bisecting a segment; bisecting an angle; constructing perpendicular lines, including the perpendicular bisector of a line segment; and constructing a line parallel to a given line through a point not on the line.

rows.heading: Make geometric constructions
rows.statement: Construct an equilateral triangle, a square, and a regular hexagon inscribed in a circle.

rows.heading: Understand similarity in terms of similarity transformations
rows.statement: Verify experimentally the properties of dilations given by a center and a scale factor:

rows.heading: Understand similarity in terms of similarity transformations
rows.statement: A dilation takes a line not passing through the center of the dilation to a parallel line, and leaves a line passing through the center unchanged.

rows.heading: Understand similarity in terms of similarity transformations
rows.statement: The dilation of a line segment is longer or shorter in the ratio given by the scale factor.

rows.heading: Understand similarity in terms of similarity transformations
rows.statement: Given two figures, use the definition of similarity in terms of similarity transformations to decide if they are similar; explain using similarity transformations the meaning of similarity for triangles as the equality of all corresponding pairs of angles and the proportionality of all corresponding pairs of sides.

rows.heading: Understand similarity in terms of similarity transformations
rows.statement: Use the properties of similarity transformations to establish the AA criterion for two triangles to be similar.

rows.heading: Prove theorems involving similarity
rows.statement: Prove theorems about triangles. Theorems include: a line parallel to one side of a triangle divides the other two proportionally, and conversely; the Pythagorean Theorem proved using triangle similarity.

rows.heading: Prove theorems involving similarity
rows.statement: Use congruence and similarity criteria for triangles to solve problems and to prove relationships in geometric figures.

rows.heading: Define trigonometric ratios and solve problems involving right triangles
rows.statement: Understand that by similarity, side ratios in right triangles are properties of the angles in the triangle, leading to definitions of trigonometric ratios for acute angles.

rows.heading: Define trigonometric ratios and solve problems involving right triangles
rows.statement: Explain and use the relationship between the sine and cosine of complementary angles.

rows.heading: Define trigonometric ratios and solve problems involving right triangles
rows.statement: Use trigonometric ratios and the Pythagorean Theorem to solve right triangles in applied problems.

rows.heading: Apply trigonometry to general triangles
rows.statement: (+) Derive the formula A = 1/2 ab sin(C) for the area of a triangle by drawing an auxiliary line from a vertex perpendicular to the opposite side.

rows.heading: Apply trigonometry to general triangles
rows.statement: (+) Prove the Laws of Sines and Cosines and use them to solve problems.

rows.heading: Apply trigonometry to general triangles
rows.statement: (+) Understand and apply the Law of Sines and the Law of Cosines to find unknown measurements in right and non-right triangles (e.g., surveying problems, resultant forces).

rows.heading: Understand and apply theorems about circles
rows.statement: Prove that all circles are similar.

rows.heading: Understand and apply theorems about circles
rows.statement: Identify and describe relationships among inscribed angles, radii, and chords. Include the relationship between central, inscribed, and circumscribed angles; inscribed angles on a diameter are right angles; the radius of a circle is perpendicular to the tangent where the radius intersects the circle.

rows.heading: Understand and apply theorems about circles
rows.statement: Construct the inscribed and circumscribed circles of a triangle, and prove properties of angles for a quadrilateral inscribed in a circle.

rows.heading: Understand and apply theorems about circles
rows.statement: (+) Construct a tangent line from a point outside a given circle to the circle.

rows.heading: Find arc lengths and areas of sectors of circles
rows.statement: Derive using similarity the fact that the length of the arc intercepted by an angle is proportional to the radius, and define the radian measure of the angle as the constant of proportionality; derive the formula for the area of a sector.

rows.heading: Translate between the geometric description and the equation for a conic section
rows.statement: Derive the equation of a circle of given center and radius using the Pythagorean Theorem; complete the square to find the center and radius of a circle given by an equation.

rows.heading: Translate between the geometric description and the equation for a conic section
rows.statement: Derive the equation of a parabola given a focus and directrix.

rows.heading: Translate between the geometric description and the equation for a conic section
rows.statement: (+) Derive the equations of ellipses and hyperbolas given the foci, using the fact that the sum or difference of distances from the foci is constant.

rows.heading: Use coordinates to prove simple geometric theorems algebraically
rows.statement: Use coordinates to prove simple geometric theorems algebraically. For example, prove or disprove that a figure defined by four given points in the coordinate plane is a rectangle; prove or disprove that the point (1, √3) lies on the circle centered at the origin and containing the point (0, 2).

rows.heading: Use coordinates to prove simple geometric theorems algebraically
rows.statement: Prove the slope criteria for parallel and perpendicular lines and use them to solve geometric problems (e.g., find the equation of a line parallel or perpendicular to a given line that passes through a given point).

rows.heading: Use coordinates to prove simple geometric theorems algebraically
rows.statement: Find the point on a directed line segment between two given points that partitions the segment in a given ratio.

rows.heading: Use coordinates to prove simple geometric theorems algebraically
rows.statement: Use coordinates to compute perimeters of polygons and areas of triangles and rectangles, e.g., using the distance formula.

rows.heading: Explain volume formulas and use them to solve problems
rows.statement: Give an informal argument for the formulas for the circumference of a circle, area of a circle, volume of a cylinder, pyramid, and cone. Use dissection arguments, Cavalieri's principle, and informal limit arguments.

rows.heading: Explain volume formulas and use them to solve problems
rows.statement: (+) Give an informal argument using Cavalieri's principle for the formulas for the volume of a sphere and other solid figures.

rows.heading: Explain volume formulas and use them to solve problems
rows.statement: Use volume formulas for cylinders, pyramids, cones, and spheres to solve problems.

rows.heading: Visualize relationships between two-dimensional and three-dimensional objects
rows.statement: Identify the shapes of two-dimensional cross-sections of three-dimensional objects, and identify three-dimensional objects generated by rotations of two-dimensional objects.

rows.heading: Apply geometric concepts in modeling situations
rows.statement: Use geometric shapes, their measures, and their properties to describe objects (e.g., modeling a tree trunk or a human torso as a cylinder).

rows.heading: Apply geometric concepts in modeling situations
rows.statement: Apply concepts of density based on area and volume in modeling situations (e.g., persons per square mile, BTUs per cubic foot).

rows.heading: Apply geometric concepts in modeling situations
rows.statement: Apply geometric methods to solve design problems (e.g., designing an object or structure to satisfy physical constraints or minimize cost; working with typographic grid systems based on ratios).

rows.heading: Summarize, represent, and interpret data on a single count or measurement variable
rows.statement: Represent data with plots on the real number line (dot plots, histograms, and box plots).

rows.heading: Summarize, represent, and interpret data on a single count or measurement variable
rows.statement: Use statistics appropriate to the shape of the data distribution to compare center (median, mean) and spread (interquartile range, standard deviation) of two or more different data sets.

rows.heading: Summarize, represent, and interpret data on a single count or measurement variable
rows.statement: Interpret differences in shape, center, and spread in the context of the data sets, accounting for possible effects of extreme data points (outliers).

rows.heading: Summarize, represent, and interpret data on a single count or measurement variable
rows.statement: Use the mean and standard deviation of a data set to fit it to a normal distribution and to estimate population percentages. Recognize that there are data sets for which such a procedure is not appropriate. Use calculators, spreadsheets, and tables to estimate areas under the normal curve.

rows.heading: Summarize, represent, and interpret data on two categorical and quantitative variables
rows.statement: Summarize categorical data for two categories in two-way frequency tables. Interpret relative frequencies in the context of the data (including joint, marginal, and conditional relative frequencies). Recognize possible associations and trends in the data.

rows.heading: Summarize, represent, and interpret data on two categorical and quantitative variables
rows.statement: Represent data on two quantitative variables on a scatter plot, and describe how the variables are related.

rows.heading: Summarize, represent, and interpret data on two categorical and quantitative variables
rows.statement: Fit a function to the data; use functions fitted to data to solve problems in the context of the data. Use given functions or choose a function suggested by the context. Emphasize linear, quadratic, and exponential models.

rows.heading: Summarize, represent, and interpret data on two categorical and quantitative variables
rows.statement: Informally assess the fit of a function by plotting and analyzing residuals.

rows.heading: Summarize, represent, and interpret data on two categorical and quantitative variables
rows.statement: Fit a linear function for a scatter plot that suggests a linear association.

rows.heading: Interpret linear models
rows.statement: Interpret the slope (rate of change) and the intercept (constant term) of a linear model in the context of the data.

rows.heading: Interpret linear models
rows.statement: Compute (using technology) and interpret the correlation coefficient of a linear fit.

rows.heading: Interpret linear models
rows.statement: Distinguish between correlation and causation.

rows.heading: Understand and evaluate random processes underlying statistical experiments
rows.statement: Understand statistics as a process for making inferences about population parameters based on a random sample from that population.

rows.heading: Understand and evaluate random processes underlying statistical experiments
rows.statement: Decide if a specified model is consistent with results from a given data-generating process, e.g., using simulation. For example, a model says a spinning coin falls heads up with probability 0.5. Would a result of 5 tails in a row cause you to question the model?

rows.heading: Make inferences and justify conclusions from sample surveys, experiments, and observational studies
rows.statement: Recognize the purposes of and differences among sample surveys, experiments, and observational studies; explain how randomization relates to each.

rows.heading: Make inferences and justify conclusions from sample surveys, experiments, and observational studies
rows.statement: Use data from a sample survey to estimate a population mean or proportion; develop a margin of error through the use of simulation models for random sampling.

rows.heading: Make inferences and justify conclusions from sample surveys, experiments, and observational studies
rows.statement: Use data from a randomized experiment to compare two treatments; use simulations to decide if differences between parameters are significant.

rows.heading: Make inferences and justify conclusions from sample surveys, experiments, and observational studies
rows.statement: Evaluate reports based on data.

rows.domain: Conditional Probability & the Rules of Probability
rows.heading: Understand independence and conditional probability and use them to interpret data
rows.statement: Describe events as subsets of a sample space (the set of outcomes) using characteristics (or categories) of the outcomes, or as unions, intersections, or complements of other events ("or," "and," "not").

rows.domain: Conditional Probability & the Rules of Probability
rows.heading: Understand independence and conditional probability and use them to interpret data
rows.statement: Understand that two events A and B are independent if the probability of A and B occurring together is the product of their probabilities, and use this characterization to determine if they are independent.

rows.domain: Conditional Probability & the Rules of Probability
rows.heading: Understand independence and conditional probability and use them to interpret data
rows.statement: Understand the conditional probability of A given B as P(A and B)/P(B), and interpret independence of A and B as saying that the conditional probability of A given B is the same as the probability of A, and the conditional probability of B given A is the same as the probability of B.

rows.domain: Conditional Probability & the Rules of Probability
rows.heading: Understand independence and conditional probability and use them to interpret data
rows.statement: Construct and interpret two-way frequency tables of data when two categories are associated with each object being classified. Use the two-way table as a sample space to decide if events are independent and to approximate conditional probabilities. For example, collect data from a random sample of students in your school on their favorite subject among math, science, and English. Estimate the probability that a randomly selected student from your school will favor science given that the student is in tenth grade. Do the same for other subjects and compare the results.

rows.domain: Conditional Probability & the Rules of Probability
rows.heading: Understand independence and conditional probability and use them to interpret data
rows.statement: Recognize and explain the concepts of conditional probability and independence in everyday language and everyday situations. For example, compare the chance of having lung cancer if you are a smoker with the chance of being a smoker if you have lung cancer.

rows.domain: Conditional Probability & the Rules of Probability
rows.heading: Use the rules of probability to compute probabilities of compound events.
rows.statement: Find the conditional probability of A given B as the fraction of B's outcomes that also belong to A, and interpret the answer in terms of the model.

rows.domain: Conditional Probability & the Rules of Probability
rows.heading: Use the rules of probability to compute probabilities of compound events.
rows.statement: Apply the Addition Rule, P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B), and interpret the answer in terms of the model.

rows.domain: Conditional Probability & the Rules of Probability
rows.heading: Use the rules of probability to compute probabilities of compound events.
rows.statement: (+) Apply the general Multiplication Rule in a uniform probability model, P(A and B) = P(A)P(B|A) = P(B)P(A|B), and interpret the answer in terms of the model.

rows.domain: Conditional Probability & the Rules of Probability
rows.heading: Use the rules of probability to compute probabilities of compound events.
rows.statement: (+) Use permutations and combinations to compute probabilities of compound events and solve problems.

rows.heading: Calculate expected values and use them to solve problems
rows.statement: (+) Define a random variable for a quantity of interest by assigning a numerical value to each event in a sample space; graph the corresponding probability distribution using the same graphical displays as for data distributions.

rows.heading: Calculate expected values and use them to solve problems
rows.statement: (+) Calculate the expected value of a random variable; interpret it as the mean of the probability distribution.

rows.heading: Calculate expected values and use them to solve problems
rows.statement: (+) Develop a probability distribution for a random variable defined for a sample space in which theoretical probabilities can be calculated; find the expected value. For example, find the theoretical probability distribution for the number of correct answers obtained by guessing on all five questions of a multiple-choice test where each question has four choices, and find the expected grade under various grading schemes.

rows.heading: Calculate expected values and use them to solve problems
rows.statement: (+) Develop a probability distribution for a random variable defined for a sample space in which probabilities are assigned empirically; find the expected value. For example, find a current data distribution on the number of TV sets per household in the United States, and calculate the expected number of sets per household. How many TV sets would you expect to find in 100 randomly selected households?

rows.heading: Use probability to evaluate outcomes of decisions
rows.statement: (+) Weigh the possible outcomes of a decision by assigning probabilities to payoff values and finding expected values.

rows.heading: Use probability to evaluate outcomes of decisions
rows.statement: Find the expected payoff for a game of chance. For example, find the expected winnings from a state lottery ticket or a game at a fast-food restaurant.

rows.heading: Use probability to evaluate outcomes of decisions
rows.statement: Evaluate and compare strategies on the basis of expected values. For example, compare a high-deductible versus a low-deductible automobile insurance policy using various, but reasonable, chances of having a minor or a major accident.

rows.heading: Use probability to evaluate outcomes of decisions
rows.statement: (+) Use probabilities to make fair decisions (e.g., drawing by lots, using a random number generator).

rows.heading: Use probability to evaluate outcomes of decisions
rows.statement: (+) Analyze decisions and strategies using probability concepts (e.g., product testing, medical testing, pulling a hockey goalie at the end of a game).

rows.heading: Key Ideas and Details
rows.statement: Cite strong and thorough textual evidence to support analysis of what the text says explicitly as well as inferences drawn from the text.

rows.heading: Key Ideas and Details
rows.statement: Determine a theme or central idea of a text and analyze in detail its development over the course of the text, including how it emerges and is shaped and refined by specific details; provide an objective summary of the text.

rows.heading: Key Ideas and Details
rows.statement: Analyze how complex characters (e.g., those with multiple or conflicting motivations) develop over the course of a text, interact with other characters, and advance the plot or develop the theme.

rows.heading: Craft and Structure
rows.statement: Determine the meaning of words and phrases as they are used in the text, including figurative and connotative meanings; analyze the cumulative impact of specific word choices on meaning and tone (e.g., how the language evokes a sense of time and place; how it sets a formal or informal tone).

rows.heading: Craft and Structure
rows.statement: Analyze how an author's choices concerning how to structure a text, order events within it (e.g., parallel plots), and manipulate time (e.g., pacing, flashbacks) create such effects as mystery, tension, or surprise.

rows.heading: Craft and Structure
rows.statement: Analyze a particular point of view or cultural experience reflected in a work of literature from outside the United States, drawing on a wide reading of world literature.

rows.heading: Integration of Knowledge and Ideas
rows.statement: Analyze the representation of a subject or a key scene in two different artistic mediums, including what is emphasized or absent in each treatment (e.g., Auden's "Musée des Beaux Arts" and Breughel's Landscape with the Fall of Icarus).

rows.heading: Integration of Knowledge and Ideas
rows.statement: Analyze how an author draws on and transforms source material in a specific work (e.g., how Shakespeare treats a theme or topic from Ovid or the Bible or how a later author draws on a play by Shakespeare).

rows.heading: Range of Reading and Level of Text Complexity
rows.statement: By the end of grade 9, read and comprehend literature, including stories, dramas, and poems, in the grades 9-10 text complexity band proficiently, with scaffolding as needed at the high end of the range. By the end of grade 10, read and comprehend literature, including stories, dramas, and poems, at the high end of the grades 9-10 text complexity band independently and proficiently.

rows.heading: Key Ideas and Details
rows.statement: Cite strong and thorough textual evidence to support analysis of what the text says explicitly as well as inferences drawn from the text, including determining where the text leaves matters uncertain.

rows.heading: Key Ideas and Details
rows.statement: Determine two or more themes or central ideas of a text and analyze their development over the course of the text, including how they interact and build on one another to produce a complex account; provide an objective summary of the text.

rows.heading: Key Ideas and Details
rows.statement: Analyze the impact of the author's choices regarding how to develop and relate elements of a story or drama (e.g., where a story is set, how the action is ordered, how the characters are introduced and developed).

rows.heading: Craft and Structure
rows.statement: Determine the meaning of words and phrases as they are used in the text, including figurative and connotative meanings; analyze the impact of specific word choices on meaning and tone, including words with multiple meanings or language that is particularly fresh, engaging, or beautiful. (Include Shakespeare as well as other authors.)

rows.heading: Craft and Structure
rows.statement: Analyze how an author's choices concerning how to structure specific parts of a text (e.g., the choice of where to begin or end a story, the choice to provide a comedic or tragic resolution) contribute to its overall structure and meaning as well as its aesthetic impact.

rows.heading: Integration of Knowledge and Ideas
rows.statement: Analyze multiple interpretations of a story, drama, or poem (e.g., recorded or live production of a play or recorded novel or poetry), evaluating how each version interprets the source text. (Include at least one play by Shakespeare and one play by an American dramatist.)

rows.heading: Integration of Knowledge and Ideas
rows.statement: Demonstrate knowledge of eighteenth-, nineteenth- and early-twentieth-century foundational works of American literature, including how two or more texts from the same period treat similar themes or topics.

rows.heading: Range of Reading and Level of Text Complexity
rows.statement: By the end of grade 11, read and comprehend literature, including stories, dramas, and poems, in the grades 11-CCR text complexity band proficiently, with scaffolding as needed at the high end of the range. By the end of grade 12, read and comprehend literature, including stories, dramas, and poems, at the high end of the grades 11-CCR text complexity band independently and proficiently.

rows.heading: Key Ideas and Details

rows.heading: Key Ideas and Details
rows.statement: Analyze how the author unfolds an analysis or series of ideas or events, including the order in which the points are made, how they are introduced and developed, and the connections that are drawn between them.

rows.heading: Craft and Structure
rows.statement: Determine the meaning of words and phrases as they are used in a text, including figurative, connotative, and technical meanings; analyze the cumulative impact of specific word choices on meaning and tone (e.g., how the language of a court opinion differs from that of a newspaper).

rows.heading: Craft and Structure
rows.statement: Analyze in detail how an author's ideas or claims are developed and refined by particular sentences, paragraphs, or larger portions of a text (e.g., a section or chapter).

rows.heading: Craft and Structure
rows.statement: Determine an author's point of view or purpose in a text and analyze how an author uses rhetoric to advance that point of view or purpose.

rows.heading: Integration of Knowledge and Ideas
rows.statement: Analyze various accounts of a subject told in different mediums (e.g., a person's life story in both print and multimedia), determining which details are emphasized in each account.

rows.heading: Integration of Knowledge and Ideas
rows.statement: Delineate and evaluate the argument and specific claims in a text, assessing whether the reasoning is valid and the evidence is relevant and sufficient; identify false statements and fallacious reasoning.

rows.heading: Integration of Knowledge and Ideas
rows.statement: Analyze seminal U.S. documents of historical and literary significance (e.g., Washington's Farewell Address, the Gettysburg Address, Roosevelt's Four Freedoms speech, King's "Letter from Birmingham Jail"), including how they address related themes and concepts.

rows.heading: Range of Reading and Level of Text Complexity
rows.statement: By the end of grade 9, read and comprehend literary nonfiction in the grades 9-10 text complexity band proficiently, with scaffolding as needed at the high end of the range. By the end of grade 10, read and comprehend literary nonfiction at the high end of the grades 9-10 text complexity band independently and proficiently.

rows.heading: Key Ideas and Details
rows.statement: Analyze a complex set of ideas or sequence of events and explain how specific individuals, ideas, or events interact and develop over the course of the text.

rows.heading: Craft and Structure
rows.statement: Determine the meaning of words and phrases as they are used in a text, including figurative, connotative, and technical meanings; analyze how an author uses and refines the meaning of a key term or terms over the course of a text (e.g., how Madison defines faction in Federalist No. 10).

rows.heading: Craft and Structure
rows.statement: Analyze and evaluate the effectiveness of the structure an author uses in his or her exposition or argument, including whether the structure makes points clear, convincing, and engaging.

rows.heading: Craft and Structure
rows.statement: Determine an author's point of view or purpose in a text in which the rhetoric is particularly effective, analyzing how style and content contribute to the power, persuasiveness or beauty of the text.

rows.heading: Integration of Knowledge and Ideas
rows.statement: Integrate and evaluate multiple sources of information presented in different media or formats (e.g., visually, quantitatively) as well as in words in order to address a question or solve a problem.

rows.heading: Integration of Knowledge and Ideas
rows.statement: Delineate and evaluate the reasoning in seminal U.S. texts, including the application of constitutional principles and use of legal reasoning (e.g., in U.S. Supreme Court majority opinions and dissents) and the premises, purposes, and arguments in works of public advocacy (e.g., The Federalist, presidential addresses).

rows.heading: Integration of Knowledge and Ideas
rows.statement: Analyze seventeenth-, eighteenth-, and nineteenth-century foundational U.S. documents of historical and literary significance (including The Declaration of Independence, the Preamble to the Constitution, the Bill of Rights, and Lincoln's Second Inaugural Address) for their themes, purposes, and rhetorical features.

rows.heading: Range of Reading and Level of Text Complexity
rows.statement: By the end of grade 11, read and comprehend literary nonfiction in the grades 11-CCR text complexity band proficiently, with scaffolding as needed at the high end of the range. By the end of grade 12, read and comprehend literary nonfiction at the high end of the grades 11-CCR text complexity band independently and proficiently.

rows.heading: Text Types and Purposes

rows.heading: Text Types and Purposes

rows.heading: Text Types and Purposes

rows.heading: Text Types and Purposes

rows.heading: Text Types and Purposes

rows.heading: Text Types and Purposes

rows.heading: Text Types and Purposes
rows.statement: Provide a conclusion that follows from and reflects on what is experienced, observed, or resolved over the course of the narrative.

rows.statement: Use technology, including the Internet, to produce, publish, and update individual or shared writing products, taking advantage of technology's capacity to link to other information and to display information flexibly and dynamically.

rows.group: Reading Standards for Literacy in History/Social Studies
rows.heading: Key Ideas and Details
rows.statement: Cite specific textual evidence to support analysis of primary and secondary sources.

rows.group: Reading Standards for Literacy in History/Social Studies
rows.heading: Key Ideas and Details
rows.statement: Determine the central ideas or information of a primary or secondary source; provide an accurate summary of the source distinct from prior knowledge or opinions.

rows.group: Reading Standards for Literacy in History/Social Studies
rows.heading: Key Ideas and Details
rows.statement: Identify key steps in a text's description of a process related to history/social studies (e.g., how a bill becomes law, how interest rates are raised or lowered).

rows.group: Reading Standards for Literacy in History/Social Studies
rows.heading: Craft and Structure
rows.statement: Determine the meaning of words and phrases as they are used in a text, including vocabulary specific to domains related to history/social studies.

rows.group: Reading Standards for Literacy in History/Social Studies
rows.heading: Craft and Structure
rows.statement: Describe how a text presents information (e.g., sequentially, comparatively, causally).

rows.group: Reading Standards for Literacy in History/Social Studies
rows.heading: Craft and Structure
rows.statement: Identify aspects of a text that reveal an author's point of view or purpose (e.g., loaded language, inclusion or avoidance of particular facts).

rows.group: Reading Standards for Literacy in History/Social Studies
rows.heading: Integration of Knowledge and Ideas
rows.statement: Integrate visual information (e.g., in charts, graphs, photographs, videos, or maps) with other information in print and digital texts.

rows.group: Reading Standards for Literacy in History/Social Studies
rows.heading: Integration of Knowledge and Ideas
rows.statement: Distinguish among fact, opinion, and reasoned judgment in a text.

rows.group: Reading Standards for Literacy in History/Social Studies
rows.heading: Integration of Knowledge and Ideas
rows.statement: Analyze the relationship between a primary and secondary source on the same topic.

rows.group: Reading Standards for Literacy in History/Social Studies
rows.heading: Range of Reading and Level of Text Complexity
rows.statement: By the end of grade 8, read and comprehend history/social studies texts in the grades 6-8 text complexity band independently and proficiently.

rows.group: Reading Standards for Literacy in History/Social Studies
rows.heading: Key Ideas and Details
rows.statement: Cite specific textual evidence to support analysis of primary and secondary sources, attending to such features as the date and origin of the information.

rows.group: Reading Standards for Literacy in History/Social Studies
rows.heading: Key Ideas and Details
rows.statement: Determine the central ideas or information of a primary or secondary source; provide an accurate summary of how key events or ideas develop over the course of the text.

rows.group: Reading Standards for Literacy in History/Social Studies
rows.heading: Key Ideas and Details
rows.statement: Analyze in detail a series of events described in a text; determine whether earlier events caused later ones or simply preceded them.

rows.group: Reading Standards for Literacy in History/Social Studies
rows.heading: Craft and Structure

rows.group: Reading Standards for Literacy in History/Social Studies
rows.heading: Craft and Structure
rows.statement: Analyze how a text uses structure to emphasize key points or advance an explanation or analysis.

rows.group: Reading Standards for Literacy in History/Social Studies
rows.heading: Craft and Structure
rows.statement: Compare the point of view of two or more authors for how they treat the same or similar topics, including which details they include and emphasize in their respective accounts.

rows.group: Reading Standards for Literacy in History/Social Studies
rows.heading: Integration of Knowledge and Ideas
rows.statement: Integrate quantitative or technical analysis (e.g., charts, research data) with qualitative analysis in print or digital text.

rows.group: Reading Standards for Literacy in History/Social Studies
rows.heading: Integration of Knowledge and Ideas
rows.statement: Assess the extent to which the reasoning and evidence in a text support the author's claims.

rows.group: Reading Standards for Literacy in History/Social Studies
rows.heading: Integration of Knowledge and Ideas
rows.statement: Compare and contrast treatments of the same topic in several primary and secondary sources.

rows.group: Reading Standards for Literacy in History/Social Studies
rows.heading: Range of Reading and Level of Text Complexity
rows.statement: By the end of grade 10, read and comprehend history/social studies texts in the grades 9-10 text complexity band independently and proficiently.

rows.group: Reading Standards for Literacy in History/Social Studies
rows.heading: Key Ideas and Details
rows.statement: Cite specific textual evidence to support analysis of primary and secondary sources, connecting insights gained from specific details to an understanding of the text as a whole.

rows.group: Reading Standards for Literacy in History/Social Studies
rows.heading: Key Ideas and Details
rows.statement: Determine the central ideas or information of a primary or secondary source; provide an accurate summary that makes clear the relationships among the key details and ideas.

rows.group: Reading Standards for Literacy in History/Social Studies
rows.heading: Key Ideas and Details
rows.statement: Evaluate various explanations for actions or events and determine which explanation best accords with textual evidence, acknowledging where the text leaves matters uncertain.

rows.group: Reading Standards for Literacy in History/Social Studies
rows.heading: Craft and Structure
rows.statement: Determine the meaning of words and phrases as they are used in a text, including analyzing how an author uses and refines the meaning of a key term over the course of a text (e.g., how Madison defines faction in Federalist No. 10).

rows.group: Reading Standards for Literacy in History/Social Studies
rows.heading: Craft and Structure
rows.statement: Analyze in detail how a complex primary source is structured, including how key sentences, paragraphs, and larger portions of the text contribute to the whole.

rows.group: Reading Standards for Literacy in History/Social Studies
rows.heading: Craft and Structure
rows.statement: Evaluate authors' differing points of view on the same historical event or issue by assessing the authors' claims, reasoning, and evidence.

rows.group: Reading Standards for Literacy in History/Social Studies
rows.heading: Integration of Knowledge and Ideas
rows.statement: Integrate and evaluate multiple sources of information presented in diverse formats and media (e.g., visually, quantitatively, as well as in words) in order to address a question or solve a problem.

rows.group: Reading Standards for Literacy in History/Social Studies
rows.heading: Integration of Knowledge and Ideas
rows.statement: Evaluate an author's premises, claims, and evidence by corroborating or challenging them with other information.

rows.group: Reading Standards for Literacy in History/Social Studies
rows.heading: Integration of Knowledge and Ideas
rows.statement: Integrate information from diverse sources, both primary and secondary, into a coherent understanding of an idea or event, noting discrepancies among sources.

rows.group: Reading Standards for Literacy in History/Social Studies
rows.heading: Range of Reading and Level of Text Complexity
rows.statement: By the end of grade 12, read and comprehend history/social studies texts in the grades 11-CCR text complexity band independently and proficiently.

rows.statement: Cite specific textual evidence to support analysis of science and technical texts.

rows.group: Reading Standards for Literacy in Science and Technical Subjects

rows.statement: Determine the central ideas or conclusions of a text; provide an accurate summary of the text distinct from prior knowledge or opinions.

rows.group: Reading Standards for Literacy in Science and Technical Subjects
rows.heading: Key Ideas and Details
rows.statement: Follow precisely a multistep procedure when carrying out experiments, taking measurements, or performing technical tasks.

rows.group: Reading Standards for Literacy in Science and Technical Subjects
rows.heading: Craft and Structure
rows.statement: Determine the meaning of symbols, key terms, and other domain-specific words and phrases as they are used in a specific scientific or technical context relevant to grades 6-8 texts and topics.

rows.group: Reading Standards for Literacy in Science and Technical Subjects
rows.heading: Craft and Structure
rows.statement: Analyze the structure an author uses to organize a text, including how the major sections contribute to the whole and to an understanding of the topic.

rows.group: Reading Standards for Literacy in Science and Technical Subjects
rows.heading: Craft and Structure
rows.statement: Analyze the author's purpose in providing an explanation, describing a procedure, or discussing an experiment in a text.

rows.group: Reading Standards for Literacy in Science and Technical Subjects
rows.heading: Integration of Knowledge and Ideas
rows.statement: Integrate quantitative or technical information expressed in words in a text with a version of that information expressed visually (e.g., in a flowchart, diagram, model, graph, or table).

rows.group: Reading Standards for Literacy in Science and Technical Subjects
rows.heading: Integration of Knowledge and Ideas
rows.statement: Distinguish among facts, reasoned judgment based on research findings, and speculation in a text.

rows.group: Reading Standards for Literacy in Science and Technical Subjects
rows.heading: Integration of Knowledge and Ideas
rows.statement: Compare and contrast the information gained from experiments, simulations, video, or multimedia sources with that gained from reading a text on the same topic.

rows.group: Reading Standards for Literacy in Science and Technical Subjects
rows.heading: Range of Reading and Level of Text Complexity
rows.statement: By the end of grade 8, read and comprehend science/technical texts in the grades 6-8 text complexity band independently and proficiently.

rows.group: Reading Standards for Literacy in Science and Technical Subjects
rows.heading: Key Ideas and Details
rows.statement: Cite specific textual evidence to support analysis of science and technical texts, attending to the precise details of explanations or descriptions.

rows.group: Reading Standards for Literacy in Science and Technical Subjects
rows.heading: Key Ideas and Details
rows.statement: Determine the central ideas or conclusions of a text; trace the text's explanation or depiction of a complex process, phenomenon, or concept; provide an accurate summary of the text.

rows.group: Reading Standards for Literacy in Science and Technical Subjects
rows.heading: Key Ideas and Details
rows.statement: Follow precisely a complex multistep procedure when carrying out experiments, taking measurements, or performing technical tasks, attending to special cases or exceptions defined in the text.

rows.group: Reading Standards for Literacy in Science and Technical Subjects
rows.heading: Craft and Structure
rows.statement: Determine the meaning of symbols, key terms, and other domain-specific words and phrases as they are used in a specific scientific or technical context relevant to grades 9-10 texts and topics.

rows.group: Reading Standards for Literacy in Science and Technical Subjects
rows.heading: Craft and Structure
rows.statement: Analyze the structure of the relationships among concepts in a text, including relationships among key terms (e.g., force, friction, reaction force, energy).

rows.group: Reading Standards for Literacy in Science and Technical Subjects
rows.heading: Craft and Structure
rows.statement: Analyze the author's purpose in providing an explanation, describing a procedure, or discussing an experiment in a text, defining the question the author seeks to address.

rows.group: Reading Standards for Literacy in Science and Technical Subjects
rows.heading: Integration of Knowledge and Ideas
rows.statement: Translate quantitative or technical information expressed in words in a text into visual form (e.g., a table or chart) and translate information expressed visually or mathematically (e.g., in an equation) into words.

rows.group: Reading Standards for Literacy in Science and Technical Subjects
rows.heading: Integration of Knowledge and Ideas
rows.statement: Assess the extent to which the reasoning and evidence in a text support the author's claim or a recommendation for solving a scientific or technical problem.

rows.group: Reading Standards for Literacy in Science and Technical Subjects
rows.heading: Integration of Knowledge and Ideas
rows.statement: Compare and contrast findings presented in a text to those from other sources (including their own experiments), noting when the findings support or contradict previous explanations or accounts.

rows.group: Reading Standards for Literacy in Science and Technical Subjects
rows.heading: Range of Reading and Level of Text Complexity
rows.statement: By the end of grade 10, read and comprehend science/technical texts in the grades 9-10 text complexity band independently and proficiently.

rows.group: Reading Standards for Literacy in Science and Technical Subjects
rows.heading: Key Ideas and Details
rows.statement: Cite specific textual evidence to support analysis of science and technical texts, attending to important distinctions the author makes and to any gaps or inconsistencies in the account.

rows.group: Reading Standards for Literacy in Science and Technical Subjects
rows.heading: Key Ideas and Details
rows.statement: Determine the central ideas or conclusions of a text; summarize complex concepts, processes, or information presented in a text by paraphrasing them in simpler but still accurate terms.

rows.group: Reading Standards for Literacy in Science and Technical Subjects
rows.heading: Key Ideas and Details
rows.statement: Follow precisely a complex multistep procedure when carrying out experiments, taking measurements, or performing technical tasks; analyze the specific results based on explanations in the text.

rows.group: Reading Standards for Literacy in Science and Technical Subjects
rows.heading: Craft and Structure
rows.statement: Determine the meaning of symbols, key terms, and other domain-specific words and phrases as they are used in a specific scientific or technical context relevant to grades 11-12 texts and topics.

rows.group: Reading Standards for Literacy in Science and Technical Subjects
rows.heading: Craft and Structure
rows.statement: Analyze how the text structures information or ideas into categories or hierarchies, demonstrating understanding of the information or ideas.

rows.group: Reading Standards for Literacy in Science and Technical Subjects
rows.heading: Craft and Structure
rows.statement: Analyze the author's purpose in providing an explanation, describing a procedure, or discussing an experiment in a text, identifying important issues that remain unresolved.

rows.group: Reading Standards for Literacy in Science and Technical Subjects
rows.heading: Integration of Knowledge and Ideas
rows.statement: Integrate and evaluate multiple sources of information presented in diverse formats and media (e.g., quantitative data, video, multimedia) in order to address a question or solve a problem.

rows.group: Reading Standards for Literacy in Science and Technical Subjects
rows.heading: Integration of Knowledge and Ideas
rows.statement: Evaluate the hypotheses, data, analysis, and conclusions in a science or technical text, verifying the data when possible and corroborating or challenging conclusions with other sources of information.

rows.group: Reading Standards for Literacy in Science and Technical Subjects
rows.heading: Integration of Knowledge and Ideas
rows.statement: Synthesize information from a range of sources (e.g., texts, experiments, simulations) into a coherent understanding of a process, phenomenon, or concept, resolving conflicting information when possible.

rows.group: Reading Standards for Literacy in Science and Technical Subjects
rows.heading: Range of Reading and Level of Text Complexity
rows.statement: By the end of grade 12, read and comprehend science/technical texts in the grades 11-CCR text complexity band independently and proficiently.

rows.group: Writing Standards for Literacy in History/Social Studies, Science, and Technical Subjects

rows.group: Writing Standards for Literacy in History/Social Studies, Science, and Technical Subjects

rows.group: Writing Standards for Literacy in History/Social Studies, Science, and Technical Subjects

rows.group: Writing Standards for Literacy in History/Social Studies, Science, and Technical Subjects

rows.group: Writing Standards for Literacy in History/Social Studies, Science, and Technical Subjects

rows.group: Writing Standards for Literacy in History/Social Studies, Science, and Technical Subjects

rows.group: Writing Standards for Literacy in History/Social Studies, Science, and Technical Subjects
rows.heading: Research to Build and Present Knowledge
rows.statement: Gather relevant information from multiple print and digital sources, using search terms effectively; assess the credibility and accuracy of each source; and quote or paraphrase the data and conclusions of others while avoiding plagiarism and following a standard format for citation.

rows.group: Writing Standards for Literacy in History/Social Studies, Science, and Technical Subjects
rows.heading: Research to Build and Present Knowledge
rows.statement: Draw evidence from informational texts to support analysis, reflection, and research.

rows.group: Writing Standards for Literacy in History/Social Studies, Science, and Technical Subjects

rows.statement: Write routinely over extended time frames (time for reflection and revision) and shorter time frames (a single sitting or a day or two) for a range of discipline-specific tasks, purposes, and audiences.

rows.group: Writing Standards for Literacy in History/Social Studies, Science, and Technical Subjects

rows.group: Writing Standards for Literacy in History/Social Studies, Science, and Technical Subjects

rows.group: Writing Standards for Literacy in History/Social Studies, Science, and Technical Subjects

rows.statement: Provide a concluding statement or section that follows from or supports the argument presented.
